# Introduction {#intro}

```{r species-image, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="*Panax quinquefolius*. Image from Wikipedia."}

wiki_page <- "American ginseng"

wiki_api <- paste0(
  "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?",
  "action=query&format=json&prop=pageimages&",
  "piprop=thumbnail&pithumbsize=1400&titles=",
  URLencode(wiki_page, reserved = TRUE))

wiki_data <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  wiki_api,
  simplifyVector = FALSE)

img_url <- wiki_data$query$pages[[1]]$thumbnail$source

dir.create("images", showWarnings = FALSE)

img_ext <- tools::file_ext(sub("\\?.*$", "", img_url))
img_file <- file.path("images", paste0("ginseng_wikipedia.", img_ext))

download.file(
  img_url,
  destfile = img_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE)

knitr::include_graphics(img_file)
```


The publication to this dataset is the following: Jennifer L. Chandler & James B. McGraw (2017). Demographic stimulation of the obligate understorey herb, Panax quinquefolius L., in response to natural forest canopy disturbances. Journal of Ecology.

The dataset contains long-term demographic census data for wild American ginseng (*Panax quinquefolius* L.) populations collected between 1998 and 2016. Formal demographic monitoring began in West Virginia in 1998 and expanded to 30 natural populations by 2004. These populations were distributed across seven U.S. states: Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia. Populations represented a range of land-use histories and eastern deciduous forest communities, providing a broad spatial and temporal dataset for studying ginseng demography and population viability. The main demographic table contains 210,384 plant-year records and 36 variables.

Each population was censused twice per year. The spring census, generally conducted from late May through June, was designed to capture population status when the greatest number of individuals were visible aboveground. During this census, individual plants were assessed for presence, leaf number, leaflet arrangement, stalk height, leaflet dimensions, reproductive status, browsing, disease, insect damage, and other plant conditions. Leaflet measurements were subsequently used to estimate total leaf area, which the authors considered the most useful continuous measure of plant size. The second census, generally conducted during the first three weeks of August, focused primarily on reproduction. Seed production was estimated from fruits on individual plants, while additional observations were made on browsing, disease, insect damage, harvest, senescence, and other changes occurring during the growing season.

Individual plants were followed repeatedly through time. Plants were marked using numbered aluminum nails placed belowground to avoid attracting attention to ginseng populations, which are subject to harvesting. Each individual was assigned an identification number within its population, while additional cluster maps, phototrails, and detailed location descriptions were used to relocate plants between censuses. Newly detected seedlings and previously missed plants were added to the census, and identifiers of dead plants were not reused. The resulting longitudinal structure allows individual survival, growth, reproduction, recruitment, browsing, harvest, and other demographic processes to be followed across years.

An important feature of the dataset is the distinction between observed and inferred plant states. For example, observed leaf number and leaf area describe plants that could be measured directly, whereas inferred leaf number and inferred leaf area were used when plants were known or assumed to be alive but their aboveground structures could not be measured. The `persistence` variable provides further information on individual status, including newly emerged seedlings, plants missing during spring or fall censuses, and individuals classified as dead. Because death in this perennial species was inferred from prolonged absence, reliable retrospective assignment of mortality was only possible through approximately 2014. The metadata explicitly caution that some individuals recorded as missing in 2015 and 2016 could subsequently have been classified as dead, which must be considered when using the final years for demographic analyses.

Overall, the dataset was developed specifically to support demographic analyses of American ginseng. Its combination of repeated individual-level observations, detailed plant size measurements, reproductive output, recruitment, mortality, browsing, harvest, and persistence information makes it suitable for analyses of vital rates, population growth, and long-term population viability.

# Data {#data}
This chapter examines the structure and quality of the original dataset and prepares the variables needed for the IPM. We first review the available measurements, missing values, and sampling coverage across populations and years. We then construct a working dataset, with particular attention to the classification of survival, dormancy, recruitment, and reproduction, as well as the reliability of demographic transitions.

## Repair encoding enough for R to handle the strings
Some location descriptions contain character encoding issues. We correct the affected entries to make them readable in R while preserving an unchanged copy of the original dataset.
```{r}
# fixes the following examplaries to displayable UTF-8 text:
# fr 1060 40Î_ 11 cm
# 257Î_ 0.5m frm 262
# fr 169 20Î_ 25 cm
loc_chr <- as.character(df_og$loc)

bad <- is.na(iconv(loc_chr, from = "", to = "UTF-8", sub = NA)) &
  !is.na(loc_chr)

loc_chr[bad] <- iconv(
  loc_chr[bad], from = "WINDOWS-1252", to = "UTF-8", sub = "?")

df_og$loc <- factor(loc_chr)
```

## Metadata
## Variable descriptions

The following variable descriptions are based on the original dataset metadata. Reported ranges refer to the value domains specified in the metadata. Numeric variables are stored as floating-point values, categorical variables as strings, and `year` as a date field (YYYY).

### Identification and sampling

- **`population`** — Unique population identifier (1–30).

- **`year`** — Year of data collection, recorded in YYYY format.

- **`id`** — Individual plant identifier, corresponding to the number on an underground aluminum marking nail (1–10003). IDs are unique within populations. Decimal identifiers (e.g., 150.1) may indicate vegetative sprouts or distinguish plants that were accidentally assigned the same number. Vegetative sprouts arise from buds on secondary or tertiary storage roots and usually persist for only a few years. When nails were lost through erosion, burial, animal activity, or harvesting, individuals were identified using location notes, previous size measurements, and cluster maps, and re-marked at the next census.

- **`cluster`** — Cluster identifier recorded in the phototrail (0.5–5704). Clusters generally represent groups of plants separated by at least 2 m from other groups. Every plant should belong to a numbered cluster.

- **`age`** — Plant age in years (0–55). Age 0 represents the year of germination. Age is recorded for seedlings followed from germination or plants subsequently aged; otherwise, it remains missing.

- **`loc`** — Location description within a cluster, used to relocate individuals alongside their underground marking nails. Particularly useful when nails were lost through erosion, harvesting, or animal disturbance.

### Vegetative measurements

- **`obs_leaf_num`** — Number of leaves observed during the spring census (1–5). May be missing if a plant was browsed or otherwise lost its aboveground structures before the census, even if it was alive.

- **`inf_leaf_num`** — Inferred number of leaves (1–5). Equals the observed leaf number when available. Otherwise, the last observed leaf number is carried forward, assuming that plants generally remain in the same leaf-number class between years. Intended for demographic classification when leaves could not be observed. According to the metadata, this value should be available for individuals subsequently confirmed alive.

- **`lflt_arr`** — Leaflet arrangement, recorded as a character sequence describing the number of leaflets on each leaf. Individual leaves may contain 1–7 leaflets. For example, `553` indicates two leaves with five leaflets and one with three, totalling 13 leaflets. Consistently recorded only after 2007. May be missing when leaves were absent or browsed below the leaflet branching point.

- **`lflt_tot`** — Total number of leaflets (0–26), calculated from the leaflet arrangement. For example, `455` represents 14 leaflets. Can serve as an alternative plant size measure, although certain leaflet combinations occur more frequently than others, producing a non-continuous distribution.

- **`stalk_ht`** — Stalk height in cm (0.1–45.5). Measured from the ground to the branching point of the leaf petioles. For one-leaf plants, measured to the base of the leaf blade. The stalk consists of fused petioles. Curled stalks and browsing can prevent reliable measurements. Because the measurement differs between one-leaf and multi-leaf plants, the original authors did not consider stalk height a suitable continuous demographic size variable.

- **`lll1`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 1, in cm (0.3–19.4). Usually the central leaflet, unless damaged.

- **`wll1`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 1, measured at its widest point, in cm (0.2–12.3).

- **`lll2`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 2, in cm (0.3–21).

- **`wll2`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 2, in cm (0.1–28).

- **`lll3`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 3, in cm (0.2–22.3).

- **`wll3`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 3, in cm (0–15.5).

- **`lll4`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 4, in cm (0–21.1).

- **`wll4`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 4, in cm (0–9.1). Rare individuals with five leaves were documented in comments and included in leaf-area estimates.

### Leaf area

- **`obs_la`** — Observed total leaf area in cm² (3.2–1381.2). Estimated using the length (`LLL`) and width (`WLL`) of the longest leaflet on each leaf, using the regression:

  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  A_{\mathrm{leaf}} ={}& -49.66435 + 6.8707463\,LLL \\
                      & + 12.626819\,WLL \\
                      & + 1.9621791(LLL-7.512)(WLL-3.637)
  \end{aligned}
  \]

  The regression was fitted using least squares in SAS JMP, with \(R^2 > 0.95\). Total observed leaf area is the sum of the estimated areas of all leaves on a plant. The original authors considered this the most suitable continuous measure of plant size.

- **`inf_la`** — Inferred leaf area in cm² (3.2–1381.2). Equals observed leaf area when the plant was measured at the spring census. When aboveground structures were absent but the plant was not classified as dead, the previously measured leaf area was carried forward as a placeholder.

  This inferred value does not necessarily represent actual leaf area. Plants might otherwise have grown, while the loss of photosynthetic tissue may reduce subsequent growth. The original authors considered carrying forward the previous measurement a compromise; alternatives include predicting expected size from growth models or interpolating between measurements from adjacent years. Inferred leaf area allows plants without measurable aboveground structures to retain a non-zero size estimate.

### Reproduction

- **`f_buds`** — Reproductive status, indicating bud or flower production. Reproduction is extremely rare in one-leaf plants, more frequent in two-leaf plants, and common among plants with three or more leaves.

- **`seeds`** — Estimated number of seeds (0–102). Counted from visible bulges in fruits during the fall census. Counts are considered reliable estimates but may miss seeds in early development or fruits dispersed before observation.

- **`red_frts`** — Number of red fruits (0–29), including partially ripened fruits. Fruits were generally counted on the plant, but fallen fruits were included when they could be confidently associated with the parent.

- **`grn_frts`** — Number of green fruits (0–53).

- **`tot_frts`** — Total number of fruits (0–54), calculated as the sum of red and green fruits.

### Harvesting and browsing

- **`harvest`** — Evidence of plant harvesting. Identified through holes where roots had been removed, loose soil, or displaced marking nails. Harvest was assigned conservatively, generally requiring similar disturbance at multiple plant locations to distinguish harvesting from animal digging. Harvesters typically targeted larger individuals.

- **`harv_time`** — Timing of harvesting. Legal harvesting seasons varied among states and throughout the study. Because the fall census generally preceded the legal harvest season, harvesting first detected during that census was classified as illegal.

- **`browse`** — Evidence of browsing, identified by torn leaf petioles or stalks. Browsing was recorded only when physical evidence remained visible. Browsed stalks were estimated to remain recognizable for approximately three weeks before decaying, meaning early-season browsing and browsing between censuses could be missed. Approximately seven weeks separated spring and fall surveys. Browsing rates derived from this variable are therefore conservative.

- **`browse_prcnt`** — Percentage of leaves removed by browsing (recorded range 25–100%). Calculated from the number of leaves lost relative to the total number of leaves, assuming equal leaf size. For example, removal of one leaf from a three-leaf plant corresponds to approximately 33%. The metadata suggest that missing values may be interpreted as 0%.

- **`browse_time`** — Timing of browsing relative to the spring census. If browsing occurred during both early and late observations, it was classified as `EARLY`, reflecting the greater demographic effects of early-season browsing.

### Persistence and demographic status

- **`persistence`** — Classification of individual persistence and demographic status. All categories except `DEAD` are considered living plants in the original dataset. The classifications distinguish missing plants, new seedlings, and confirmed mortality.

  **`DEAD` — Dead individuals**

  Death was inferred from prolonged absence rather than directly observed. The required duration depended on plant size:

  - New seedlings missing by fall of their first year were classified as dead if also absent the following spring.
  - Established one-leaf plants were classified as dead when absent during the fall two years earlier and the preceding spring.
  - Two-leaf plants were classified as dead after two consecutive spring absences (`MIA S`).
  - Plants with three or more leaves were classified as dead when missing during fall three seasons earlier and during two subsequent spring censuses.

  In 2016, roots of some missing three-leaf plants were searched for near their tags. If no living root was found, death could be assigned after two seasons.

  Because mortality was determined retrospectively, **reliable death classification was possible only through 2014**. Some plants classified as missing in 2015–2016 may have been reclassified as dead with additional observations.

  **`NS` — New seedling**

  A newly established, one-leaf individual in its first year. Seedlings were identified when at least three of five criteria were met:

  1. Seed coat still attached to the plant.
  2. Absence of an obvious branching node on the stalk.
  3. Small-diameter white root below the seed coat.
  4. Narrow central leaflet with a high length-to-width ratio.
  5. Absence of an existing tag or previous database record.

  Most seedlings emerged before the spring census, although occasional germination between spring and fall was documented.

  New seedlings were recorded within 2 m of previously established plants. Based on earlier seed-dispersal experiments, the original authors estimated that this sampling approach detected approximately **90% of new recruits**. They suggested that fecundity estimates could be adjusted for the remaining 10%, although dispersal by thrushes could increase the proportion of seedlings missed.

  **`MIA S` — Missing in spring**

  The plant's aboveground structures were absent during the spring census, regardless of whether browsing evidence was present. Consequently, leaf area could not be measured directly.

  **`MIA F` — Missing in fall**

  Individuals present during the spring census but absent during the fall census.

### Insects and disease

- **`insect`** — Evidence of insect damage, generally recorded when at least 5% of leaf area had been removed. Damage types were not distinguished.

- **`thrips`** — Evidence of thrips damage, identified by small white spots on leaf surfaces.

- **`fungal`** — Presence of fungal disease.

- **`fungal_cat`** — Category of fungal disease.

## Properties of downloaded data
```{r}
meta_data <- tibble(variable = names(df_og)) %>%
  mutate(
    class = map_chr(
      variable, ~ paste(class(df_og[[.x]]), collapse = ", ")),
    n = nrow(df_og),
    n_missing = map_int(variable, ~ sum(is.na(df_og[[.x]]))),
    pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / n, 2),
    n_unique = map_int(
      variable, ~ n_distinct(df_og[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)),
    minimum = map_chr(variable, function(x) {
      z <- df_og[[x]]
      if (!is.numeric(z) || all(is.na(z))) return(NA_character_)
      as.character(min(z, na.rm = TRUE))
    }),
    maximum = map_chr(variable, function(x) {
      z <- df_og[[x]]
      if (!is.numeric(z) || all(is.na(z))) return(NA_character_)
      as.character(max(z, na.rm = TRUE))
    }),
    encoding_issues = map_int(variable, function(x) {
      z <- df_og[[x]]
      if (!is.character(z) && !is.factor(z)) return(0L)
      
      z <- as.character(z)
      sum(
        is.na(iconv(z, from = "", to = "UTF-8", sub = NA)) &
          !is.na(z))
    })) %>%
  left_join(meta_ref, by = "variable")

meta_data
```

## Sampling structure over time
Sampling coverage varies across populations and years, particularly during the initial years when additional populations entered the study. The following figure shows the temporal coverage at the state, population, and cluster levels, based on the records available in the dataset.
```{r}
df_sampling <- df_og %>%
  left_join(
    df_meta %>%
      select(population, state),
    by = "population") %>%
  mutate(
    population_id = paste0(state, " - Pop ", population),
    cluster_id = paste0("Pop ", population, " - Cl ", cluster))
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}
p_state <- df_sampling %>%

  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = population_id)) +

# Cluster ---------------------------------------------------------------------

p_cluster <- df_sampling %>%
  filter(!is.na(cluster)) %>%
  distinct(year, population, cluster, cluster_id) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = factor(cluster))) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ population, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1998, 2016, 3)) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Cluster",
    title = "Clusters within populations") +
  theme_bw()


# Combined overview -----------------------------------------------------------

p_state / p_population / p_cluster +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3, 7))
```

## Variables
We classify the original variables according to their potential role in the IPM, distinguishing structural information, plant size, demographic status, reproduction, and potential covariates. This provides an overview of which measurements are relevant for the subsequent models.
```{r}
df_ipm_variables <- meta_data %>%
  mutate(
    ipm_role = case_when(
      variable %in% c("population", "year", "id", "cluster") ~
        "Structure",
      variable %in% c(
        "obs_la", "inf_la", "obs_leaf_num", "inf_leaf_num",
        "lflt_tot", "stalk_ht") ~
        "Size / growth",
      variable %in% c(
        "lll1", "wll1", "lll2", "wll2",
        "lll3", "wll3", "lll4", "wll4") ~
        "Raw size measurement",
      variable == "persistence" ~
        "Survival / dormancy / recruitment",
      variable == "f_buds" ~
        "Flowering",
      variable %in% c(
        "seeds", "red_frts", "grn_frts", "tot_frts") ~
        "Fecundity",
      variable %in% c(
        "browse", "browse_prcnt", "browse_time",
        "harvest", "harv_time", "insect", "thrips",
        "fungal", "fungal_cat", "age") ~
        "Potential covariate",
      variable %in% c("loc", "lflt_arr") ~
        "Not core IPM",
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified"))

df_ipm_variables
```

## Working data
We construct the working dataset using inferred leaf area (inf_la) as the continuous measure of plant size, retaining size estimates where direct measurements were unavailable.

We derive demographic states from the persistence variable. All persistence classes except DEAD are treated as alive, while MIA S identifies dormant individuals and NS identifies new seedlings.

**Dormancy and survival cutoff.** Because mortality classification relies on subsequent observations, survival and dormancy cannot be reliably determined for the final two years (2015–2016). We therefore apply a two-year cutoff, restricting survival and dormancy transitions to consecutive observations ending no later than 2014. Growth transitions remain available for consecutive years beyond this cutoff.

**Reproductive variables.** Flowering is identified from recorded reproductive status or positive fruit or seed production. We retain fruit presence, total fruit number, and seed number as separate variables for the subsequent fecundity models.
```{r}
dormancy_cutoff <- 2
last_reliable_year <- max(df_og$year, na.rm = TRUE) - dormancy_cutoff

df_work <- df_og %>%
  dplyr::left_join(df_meta, by = "population") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(population, id, year) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    persistence = trimws(persistence),
    size = inf_la,
    recruit = as.integer(persistence == "NS"),
    alive = dplyr::case_when(
      persistence == "DEAD" ~ 0,
      !is.na(persistence) ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    dormant = dplyr::case_when(
      persistence == "MIA S" ~ 1,
      persistence == "DEAD" ~ NA_real_,
      !is.na(persistence) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(population, id) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    year_t1 = dplyr::lead(year),
    size_t1 = dplyr::lead(size),
    persistence_t1 = dplyr::lead(persistence),
    survives = dplyr::lead(alive),
    dormant_t1 = dplyr::lead(dormant)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    consecutive = year_t1 == year + 1L,
    reliable_demography = consecutive &
      year_t1 <= last_reliable_year,
    survives = dplyr::if_else(
      reliable_demography, survives, NA_real_),
    dormant_t0 = dplyr::if_else(
      year <= last_reliable_year, dormant, NA_real_),
    dormant_t1 = dplyr::if_else(
      reliable_demography, dormant_t1, NA_real_),
    size_t1 = dplyr::if_else(
      consecutive, size_t1, NA_real_),
    logsize_t0 = log(size),
    logsize_t1 = log(size_t1),
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3,
    f_buds = na_if(trimws(f_buds), ""),
    flower = case_when(
      coalesce(seeds > 0, FALSE) |
        coalesce(tot_frts > 0, FALSE) ~ 1,
      f_buds == "Y" ~ 1,
      f_buds == "N" ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    fruit = case_when(
      tot_frts > 0 ~ 1,
      tot_frts == 0 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    fruit_nr = tot_frts,
    seed_nr = seeds) %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    size_t0 = size,
    persistence_t0 = persistence) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, cluster, id, year, year_t1,
    persistence_t0, persistence_t1,
    dormant_t0, dormant_t1,
    size_t0, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    survives, recruit, consecutive, reliable_demography,
    flower, fruit, fruit_nr, seed_nr,
    f_buds, seeds, red_frts, grn_frts, tot_frts)

```

## Inferred sizes

As shown above, the dataset provides inferred sizes, e.g. inferred number of leaves or inferred leaf areas. As describes by the authors, at times sizes did not receive data. Those datapoints were "inferred" by taking the last know size measurement and mirror them into the observation in question. The last known measurement might be from the same year (in which case I am unsure why it would not be there already and how they brought several observations within year to the now given "one census") or else from previous years. The author reason that, especially for leave numbers, the plant rarely changes over time. The question remains of how many datapoint where curated in that way.

```{r}
df_og %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_obs = sum(!is.na(obs_la)),
    n_inf = sum(!is.na(inf_la)),
    n_both = sum(!is.na(obs_la) & !is.na(inf_la)),
    n_inf_only = sum(is.na(obs_la) & !is.na(inf_la)),
    n_obs_only = sum(!is.na(obs_la) & is.na(inf_la)),
    n_neither = sum(is.na(obs_la) & is.na(inf_la)))
```

# Mean IPM, basic {#ipm_mean_zero}

## Introduction
In this chapter, we construct a basic mean IPM as a starting point for the more detailed models developed later. We estimate survival, growth, and recruitment using data pooled across populations and years. The model includes a single continuous size state, with recruitment treated as size-independent and no explicit dormancy or reproductive stages. We then calculate the asymptotic population growth rate and compare it with the observed population growth rates.

## Specifications
### Vital model
```{r}
v_mod_set_su <- c()
v_mod_set_gr <- c()
```

## Data
```{r}
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0(v_head, '_', v_sp_abb, '_df_workdata.csv'))) %>% 
  filter(state == v_states)

required_cols <- c(
  'state', 'population', 'id', 'year', 'year_t1', 'size_t0', 'size_t1',
  'logsize_t0', 'logsize_t1', 'logsize_t0_2', 'logsize_t0_3', 'survives',
  'recruit', 'consecutive', 'reliable_demography', 'persistence_t0')

missing_cols <- setdiff(required_cols, names(df))
if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
  stop(paste(
    'Missing columns in working data:',
    paste(missing_cols, collapse = ', ')))}
```

## Vital rates
For survival and growth, we consider four model structures: intercept-only, linear, quadratic, and cubic relationships with log leaf area. Model selection is based on AICc, with the option to manually specify a model instead.
### Survival
#### Data
```{r}
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    reliable_demography,
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, id, year, size_t0, survives,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)
```

#### Model
```{r}
mod_su_0 <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mod_su_1 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mod_su_2 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mod_su_3 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_0, mod_su_1, mod_su_2, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_su, weights = TRUE, sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- mods_su_sorted[1]
  v_mod_su_index <- mod_su_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_su + 1
  v_mod_su_index <- v_mod_set_su}

mod_su_bestfit <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_bestfit]]

mod_su_bestfit
mods_su_dAICc
```

#### Plot
```{r}
df_su_newdata <- tibble(
  logsize_t0 = seq(
    min(df_su$logsize_t0),
    max(df_su$logsize_t0),
    length.out = 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3)

df_su_newdata$predicted <- predict(
  mod_su_bestfit,
  newdata = df_su_newdata,
  type = 'response')

fig_su_line <- ggplot(
  df_su,
  aes(x = logsize_t0, y = survives)) +
  geom_jitter(
    height = 0.05, width = 0,
    alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(
    data = df_su_newdata,
    aes(y = predicted),
    linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = 'Survival probability by size',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x = expression('log(leaf area)'[t0]),
    y = 'Probability of survival') +
  theme_bw()


df_su_bindata <- plot_binned_prop(
  df_su, 10, logsize_t0, survives)

fig_su_bin <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = df_su_bindata,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = survives)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    data = df_su_bindata,
    aes(
      x = logsize_t0,
      ymin = lwr,
      ymax = upr),
    width = 0.1) +
  geom_line(
    data = df_su_newdata,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = predicted),
    linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = expression('log(leaf area)'[t0]),
    y = '') +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1)

fig_su <- fig_su_line + fig_su_bin + plot_layout()
fig_su
```

```{r}
  v_mod_gr_index <- mod_gr_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_gr_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_gr + 1
  v_mod_gr_index <- v_mod_set_gr}

mod_gr_bestfit <- mods_gr[[mod_gr_index_bestfit]]

mod_gr_bestfit
mods_gr_dAICc
```

#### Plot
```{r}
df_gr_newdata <- tibble(
  logsize_t0 = seq(
    min(df_gr$logsize_t0),
    max(df_gr$logsize_t0),
    length.out = 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3)

df_gr_newdata <- cbind(

fig_gr <- ggplot(
```

#### Growth variance
```{r}
mod_gr_x <- fitted(mod_gr_bestfit)
mod_gr_y <- resid(mod_gr_bestfit)^2

mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x),
  start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(
    maxiter = 1000, tol = 1e-6, warnOnly = TRUE))
```

### Recruitment
Unlike survival and growth, recruitment is estimated at the population-year level.

We count living individuals with positive size in year (t) and newly recorded seedlings in year (t+1), retaining only transitions where the population was sampled in both years. A negative-binomial model with an offset for the number of individuals estimates the mean recruitment rate per individual.

This population-level estimate is then applied uniformly to all individuals in the IPM, regardless of their size or reproductive status. Thus, recruitment is assumed to be proportional to the number of established individuals, without explicitly modelling seed production.
```{r}
# Constant mean recruitment is estimated as recruits per established plant.
# Parent abundance is measured in year t0 and recruits enter in year t1.

df_re_parent <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(persistence_t0),
    persistence_t0 != 'DEAD',
    size_t0 > 0) %>%
  group_by(population, year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_parents = n_distinct(id),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(year_t1 = year + 1L)

# Years in which a population was actually sampled.
df_re_sampled <- df %>%
  distinct(population, year) %>%
  rename(year_t1 = year)

# New seedlings observed in year t1.
df_re_count <- df %>%
  filter(recruit == 1) %>%
  count(population, year, name = 'nr_recruits') %>%
  rename(year_t1 = year)

# Keep only population-year transitions with sampling at both t0 and t1.
df_re <- df_re_parent %>%
  inner_join(
    df_re_sampled,
    by = c('population', 'year_t1')) %>%
  left_join(
    df_re_count,
    by = c('population', 'year_t1')) %>%
  mutate(
    nr_recruits = replace_na(nr_recruits, 0L))


fig_re_hist <- ggplot(df_re, aes(x = nr_recruits)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = -0.5,
                 fill = "grey60", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of recruitment",
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x = "Number of recruits",
    y = "Frequency") +
  theme_bw()

fig_re_hist
```

#### Recruitment probability

```{r}
df_re_prob <- df_re %>%

mod_re_prob <- glm(

summary(mod_re_prob)


df_re_prob_newdata <- tibble(

pred_re_prob <- predict(

df_re_prob_newdata <- df_re_prob_newdata %>%

  geom_ribbon(

df_re_prob_bindata <- plot_binned_prop(

fig_re_prob_bin <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = df_re_prob_bindata,

  geom_errorbar(
    data = df_re_prob_bindata,

    x = expression('Established individuals'[t0]),
    y = 'Probability of recruitment') +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_bw()

fig_re_prob + fig_re_prob_bin + plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```

## Estimates
```{r}
# Exporting parameter estimates
# Growth
pars_gr <- tibble(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_gr_bestfit)),
  value = unname(coef(mod_gr_bestfit))) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = if_else(
      coefficient == '(Intercept)', 'b0', coefficient))

pars_gr_var <- tibble(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_gr_var)),
  value = unname(coef(mod_gr_var)))

pars_gr <- bind_rows(pars_gr, pars_gr_var)

# Survival
pars_su <- tibble(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_su_bestfit)),
  value = unname(coef(mod_su_bestfit))) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = if_else(
      coefficient == '(Intercept)', 'b0', coefficient))

# Recruitment and mesh limits
pars_other <- tibble(
  coefficient = c(
    'recr_sz', 'recr_sd', 'max_siz', 'min_siz', 'fecu_b0'),
  value = c(
    mean(df_re_size$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd(df_re_size$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    max(df_gr$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    min(df_gr$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    fecu_mean))
```

## Building IPM
```{r}
extr_value <- function(x, field) {
  subset(x, coefficient == field)$value
}

pars <- Filter(function(x) length(x) > 0, list(
  prefix = v_script_prefix,
  species = v_species,
  surv_b0 = extr_value(pars_su, 'b0'),
  surv_b1 = extr_value(pars_su, 'logsize_t0'),
  surv_b2 = extr_value(pars_su, 'logsize_t0_2'),
  surv_b3 = extr_value(pars_su, 'logsize_t0_3'),
  grow_b0 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'b0'),
  grow_b1 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'logsize_t0'),
  grow_b2 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'logsize_t0_2'),
  grow_b3 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'logsize_t0_3'),
  a = extr_value(pars_gr, 'a'),
  b = extr_value(pars_gr, 'b'),
  fecu_b0 = extr_value(pars_other, 'fecu_b0'),
  recr_sz = extr_value(pars_other, 'recr_sz'),
  recr_sd = extr_value(pars_other, 'recr_sd'),
  L = extr_value(pars_other, 'min_siz'),
  U = extr_value(pars_other, 'max_siz'),
  mat_siz = 200,
  mod_gr_index = v_mod_gr_index,
  mod_su_index = v_mod_su_index))
```

### IPM functions
```{r}
grow_sd <- function(x, pars) {
  sqrt(pars$a * exp(pars$b * x))
}

# Growth from size x to size y.
gxy <- function(x, y, pars, num_pars = v_mod_gr_index) {
  mean_value <- 0
  for (i in 0:num_pars) {
    param_name <- paste0('grow_b', i)
    if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
      mean_value <- mean_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}
  }
  sd_value <- grow_sd(x, pars)
  dnorm(y, mean = mean_value, sd = sd_value)
}

inv_logit <- function(x) {
  exp(x) / (1 + exp(x))
}

# Survival of an x-sized individual to t1.
sx <- function(x, pars, num_pars = v_mod_su_index) {
  survival_value <- pars$surv_b0
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('surv_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        survival_value <- survival_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}
    }
  }
  inv_logit(survival_value)
}

# Survival-growth transition.
pxy <- function(x, y, pars) {
  sx(x, pars) * gxy(x, y, pars)
}

# Constant mean fecundity distributed across recruit sizes.
fy <- function(y, pars, h) {
  n_recr <- pars$fecu_b0
  recr_sd <- max(h / 10, pars$recr_sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  recr_y <- dnorm(y, pars$recr_sz, recr_sd) * h
  recr_y <- recr_y / sum(recr_y)
  n_recr * recr_y
}
```

### Kernel
We construct a size-structured kernel using 200 mesh points. The survival-growth component describes transitions of established individuals, while the fecundity component adds new recruits according to their estimated size distribution.

Because recruitment is independent of parent size, the fecundity contribution is identical across all parent-size classes. We also correct the growth distribution at the mesh boundaries to retain transitions that would otherwise fall outside the modelled size range.
```{r}
kernel <- function(pars) {
  n <- pars$mat_siz
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  Fmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Fmat[] <- matrix(fy(y, pars, h), n, n)

  Smat <- sx(y, pars)

  Gmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Gmat[] <- t(outer(y, y, gxy, pars)) * h

  Tmat <- matrix(0, n, n)

  for (i in seq_len(n / 2)) {
    Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  for (i in ((n / 2) + 1):n) {
    Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  k_yx <- Fmat + Tmat

  list(
    k_yx = k_yx,
    Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat,
    Gmat = Gmat,
    meshpts = y)
}

lambda_ipm <- function(i) {
  Re(eigen(kernel(i)$k_yx)$values[1])
}
```

## Outcome
### Mean IPM population growth rate
```{r}
lam_mean <- lambda_ipm(pars)
lam_mean
```

### Observed population growth rate
```{r}
# Count living individuals in each sampled population-year.
df_pop_n <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(persistence_t0),
    persistence_t0 != 'DEAD') %>%
  group_by(population, year) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n_distinct(id),
    .groups = 'drop')

pop_counts_t0 <- df_pop_n %>%
  transmute(
    population,
    year = year + 1L,
    n_t0 = n)

pop_counts_t1 <- df_pop_n %>%
  transmute(
    population,
    year,
    n_t1 = n)

pop_counts <- inner_join(
  pop_counts_t0,
  pop_counts_t1,
  by = c('population', 'year')) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_t0 = sum(n_t0),
    n_t1 = sum(n_t1),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(
    obs_pgr = n_t1 / n_t0)

lam_mean_count <- exp(mean(log(pop_counts$obs_pgr), na.rm = TRUE))
lam_mean_overall <- sum(pop_counts$n_t1) / sum(pop_counts$n_t0)

lam_mean_count
lam_mean_overall
```

## Building the IPM with ipmr
```{r}
proto_ipm_p <- init_ipm(
  sim_gen = 'simple',
  di_dd = 'di',
  det_stoch = 'det') %>%
  define_kernel(
    name = 'P',
    family = 'CC',
    formula = s * g,
    s = plogis(
      surv_b0 +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 1) surv_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 2) surv_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 3) surv_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    mu_g = grow_b0 +
      (if (mod_gr_index >= 1) grow_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
      (if (mod_gr_index >= 2) grow_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
      (if (mod_gr_index >= 3) grow_b3 * size_1^3 else 0),
    g = dnorm(size_2, mu_g, grow_sig),
    grow_sig = sqrt(a * exp(b * size_1)),
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('size')),
    evict_cor = TRUE,
    evict_fun = truncated_distributions(
      fun = 'norm', target = 'g')) %>%
  define_kernel(
    name = 'F',
    family = 'CC',
    formula = fecu_b0 * r_d,
    r_d = dnorm(size_2, recr_sz, recr_sd),
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('size')),
    evict_cor = TRUE,
    evict_fun = truncated_distributions('norm', 'r_d')) %>%
  define_impl(
    make_impl_args_list(
      kernel_names = c('P', 'F'),
      int_rule = rep('midpoint', 2),
      state_start = rep('size', 2),
      state_end = rep('size', 2))) %>%
  define_domains(
    size = c(
      pars$L,
      pars$U,
      pars$mat_siz)) %>%
  define_pop_state(
    n_size = rep(
      1 / pars$mat_siz,
      pars$mat_siz))

ipmr_p <- make_ipm(
  proto_ipm = proto_ipm_p,
  iterations = 200)

lam_mean_ipmr <- lambda(ipmr_p)

lam_out <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(lam_mean_ipmr),
  value = lam_mean_ipmr)

lam_out_wide <- as.list(
  pivot_wider(
    lam_out,
    names_from = 'coefficient',
    values_from = 'value'))

lam_out_wide
```

# Mean IPM {#ipm_mean}

## Introduction
In this chapter, we extend the basic mean IPM by explicitly modelling dormancy and separating recruitment into its reproductive components. Alongside survival and growth, we estimate dormancy entry, dormant survival, reactivation, flowering probability, seed production, and the seed-to-recruit transition. The model still uses mean vital rates pooled across populations and years, but now distinguishes active plants, dormant individuals, and seeds.

## Specifications
### Vital model
```{r}
v_mod_set_su   <- c()
v_mod_set_gr   <- c()
v_mod_set_do   <- c()
v_mod_set_fl   <- c()
v_mod_set_se   <- c()
v_mod_set_se_n <- c()
```

## Data
```{r}
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0(v_head, '_', v_sp_abb, '_df_workdata.csv'))) %>% 
  filter(state == v_states)
```

## Vital rates
For survival, growth, dormancy entry, flowering, and seed production, we consider intercept-only, linear, quadratic, and cubic relationships with log leaf area. Model selection is based on AICc, with the option to manually specify a model instead.

Unlike the basic IPM, survival is estimated for initially active individuals, while growth is restricted to individuals remaining active in consecutive years.
### Survival
#### Data
```{r}
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    reliable_demography,
    dormant_t0 == 0,
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, id, year, size_t0, survives,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)
```

#### Model
```{r}
mod_su_0 <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mod_su_1 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mod_su_2 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mod_su_3 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3,
  data = df_su, family = 'binomial')

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_0, mod_su_1, mod_su_2, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_su, weights = TRUE, sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- mods_su_sorted[1]
  v_mod_su_index <- mod_su_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_su + 1
  v_mod_su_index <- v_mod_set_su}

mod_su_bestfit <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_bestfit]]

mod_su_bestfit
mods_su_dAICc
```

#### Plot
```{r}
df_su_newdata <- tibble(
  logsize_t0 = seq(
    min(df_su$logsize_t0),
    max(df_su$logsize_t0),
    length.out = 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3)

df_su_newdata$predicted <- predict(
  mod_su_bestfit,
  newdata = df_su_newdata,
  type = 'response')

fig_su_line <- ggplot(
  df_su,

  geom_jitter(

    aes(
      x = logsize_t0,
      ymin = lwr,
      ymax = upr),
    width = 0.1) +
  geom_line(
    data = df_su_newdata,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = predicted),
    linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = expression('log(leaf area)'[t0]),
    y = '') +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1)

fig_su <- fig_su_line + fig_su_bin + plot_layout()
fig_su
```

### Growth variance
```{r}
mod_gr_x <- fitted(mod_gr_bestfit)
mod_gr_y <- resid(mod_gr_bestfit)^2

mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x),
  start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(
    maxiter = 1000, tol = 1e-6, warnOnly = TRUE))
```


### Dormancy entry 
Dormancy entry is estimated as the probability that an active individual becomes dormant in the following year, conditional on survival. We model this transition as a function of initial plant size, using only observations with reliable demographic information.


#### Data
```{r}
df_do <- df %>%
  filter(
    reliable_demography,
    dormant_t0 == 0,
    survives == 1,
    !is.na(dormant_t1),
    size_t0 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0)) %>%
  mutate(enter_dormancy = dormant_t1) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, year, size_t0, enter_dormancy,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)

df_do %>%
  count(enter_dormancy)
```

#### Model
```{r}

  data = df_do, family = "binomial")

  data = df_do, family = "binomial")

mod_do_2 <- glm(
  enter_dormancy ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2,
  data = df_do, family = "binomial")

mod_do_3 <- glm(
  enter_dormancy ~
    logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3,
  data = df_do, family = "binomial")

mods_do <- list(
  mod_do_0, mod_do_1, mod_do_2, mod_do_3)

mods_do_dAICc <- AICctab(
  mods_do, weights = TRUE, sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_do_sorted <- order(mods_do_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_do) == 0) {
  mod_do_index_bestfit <- mods_do_sorted[1]
  v_mod_do_index <- mod_do_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_do_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_do + 1
  v_mod_do_index <- v_mod_set_do
}

mod_do_bestfit <- mods_do[[mod_do_index_bestfit]]

mod_do_bestfit
mods_do_dAICc
```

### Dormancy entry vs reactivation size
```{r}
df_ra_size <- df %>%
```

### Dormant survival and reactivation
For dormant individuals, survival and reactivation are estimated separately using intercept-only binomial models. Both probabilities are treated as size-independent, since aboveground size cannot be measured during dormancy.

For individuals returning to the active state, we estimate a reactivation size distribution from their observed leaf area upon reappearance. This distribution is used to assign sizes to reactivated individuals in the IPM.
```{r}
df_ra <- df %>%
  filter(
    reliable_demography,
    dormant_t0 == 1,
    !is.na(survives))

mod_dorm_su <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_ra,
  family = "binomial")

p_dorm_survival <- predict(
  mod_dorm_su,
  newdata = data.frame(x = 1),
  type = "response")[1]


df_ra <- df_ra %>%
  filter(
    survives == 1,
    !is.na(dormant_t1)) %>%
  mutate(
    reactivate = as.integer(dormant_t1 == 0))

mod_ra <- glm(
  reactivate ~ 1,
  data = df_ra,
  family = "binomial")

p_reactivate <- predict(
  mod_ra,
  newdata = data.frame(x = 1),
  type = "response")[1]


df_ra_size <- df %>%
  filter(
    reliable_demography,
    dormant_t0 == 1,
    survives == 1,
    dormant_t1 == 0,
    size_t1 > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_reactivate = log(size_t1))

react_sz <- mean(
  df_ra_size$logsize_reactivate,
  na.rm = TRUE)

react_sd <- sigma(mod_ra_size)
```

### Flowering probability
We separate reproductive output into three components: flowering probability, the probability of producing at least one seed conditional on flowering, and the number of seeds conditional on positive seed production. Each component is modelled as a function of plant size. Their product gives the expected seed production of an active individual.
#### Data
```{r}
df_fl <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(flower),
    size_t0 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, id, year, size_t0, flower,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)
```

#### Model
```{r}
mod_fl_0 <- glm(
  flower ~ 1,
  data = df_fl,
  family = "binomial")

mod_fl_1 <- glm(
  flower ~ logsize_t0,
  data = df_fl,
  family = "binomial")

mod_fl_2 <- glm(
  flower ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2,
  data = df_fl,
  family = "binomial")

mod_fl_3 <- glm(
  flower ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3,
  data = df_fl,
  family = "binomial")

mods_fl <- list(
  mod_fl_0, mod_fl_1, mod_fl_2, mod_fl_3)

mods_fl_dAICc <- AICctab(
  mods_fl,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_fl_sorted <- order(mods_fl_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_fl) == 0) {
  mod_fl_index_bestfit <- mods_fl_sorted[1]
  v_mod_fl_index <- mod_fl_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_fl_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_fl + 1
  v_mod_fl_index <- v_mod_set_fl
}

mod_fl_bestfit <- mods_fl[[mod_fl_index_bestfit]]

mod_fl_bestfit
mods_fl_dAICc
```

#### Plot
```{r}
df_fl_newdata <- tibble(
  logsize_t0 = seq(
    min(df_fl$logsize_t0),
    max(df_fl$logsize_t0),
    length.out = 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3)

df_fl_newdata$flower <- predict(
```

#### Seed model comparison with upper Logistic plateau model

To model the probability of seed production conditional on flowering,
a three-parameter logistic model with an estimated upper asymptote
was fitted using a binomial likelihood.

$$
p(x) = \frac{A}{1 + \exp(-(b_0 + b_1 x))}
$$

where:
- $x$ is log-transformed leaf area.
- $b_0$ is the intercept.
- $b_1$ controls the relationship between size and seed production.
- $A$ is the estimated maximum probability (upper plateau).

Unlike standard logistic regression, which approaches a probability
of 1, this model allows the probability to level off below 1.
The upper asymptote is estimated from the data rather than fixed.

The model was fitted by maximum likelihood, with
$A = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a)$ to constrain the plateau between 0 and 1.

```{r}
mod_se_plateau <- bbmle::mle2(
  seed_prod ~ dbinom(
    size = 1,
    prob = plogis(a) * plogis(b0 + b1 * logsize_t0)),
  data = df_se,
  start = list(
    a = 0,
    b0 = unname(coef(mod_se_1)[1]),
    b1 = unname(coef(mod_se_1)[2])))

summary(mod_se_plateau)

# Estimated upper plateau
plogis(coef(mod_se_plateau)["a"])

df_se_compare <- df_se_newdata %>%
  mutate(
    linear = predict(mod_se_1, newdata = ., type = "response"),
    quadratic = predict(mod_se_2, newdata = ., type = "response"),
    plateau = plogis(coef(mod_se_plateau)["a"]) *
      plogis(coef(mod_se_plateau)["b0"] +
               coef(mod_se_plateau)["b1"] * logsize_t0)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(linear, quadratic, plateau),
    names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted")

fig_se_compare <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = df_se_bindata,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = seed_prod)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    data = df_se_bindata,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr),
    width = 0.1) +
  geom_line(
    data = df_se_compare,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = predicted, color = model),
    linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Seed production probability by size",
    x = expression("log(leaf area)"[t0]),
    y = "Probability of producing seeds",
    color = "Model") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_bw()

fig_se_compare

```

### Seed to recruit transition
Unlike the preceding reproductive processes, the seed-to-recruit transition is estimated at the population-year level, since recruits cannot be assigned to individual parent plants.

We sum observed seed production within each population and year and relate it to the number of new seedlings observed two years later. A negative-binomial model with an offset for total seed production estimates the expected number of recruits per observed seed. Only observations with positive seed totals are used to fit this relationship.

This population-level estimate is applied to the seeds produced by individual plants in the IPM. Recruitment therefore depends on individual seed production, while the subsequent seed-to-recruit transition remains size-independent.
```{r}
df_re_seed <- df %>%
  group_by(
    population, year) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_seeds = sum(
      seed_nr,
      na.rm = TRUE),
    nr_seed_obs = sum(
      !is.na(seed_nr)),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(
    nr_seed_obs > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = year + 1L)


# Number of recruits per sampled population and year.
df_re_sampled <- df %>%
  distinct(
    population, year)

df_re_count <- df %>%
  filter(
    recruit == 1) %>%
  count(
    population, year,
    name = "nr_recruits")

df_re_count <- df_re_sampled %>%
  left_join(
    df_re_count,
    by = c(
      "population",
      "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    nr_recruits = replace_na(
      nr_recruits,
      0L))


# Match seed production at t to recruits at t + 1.
df_re <- df_re_seed %>%
  inner_join(
    df_re_count,
    by = c(
      "population",
      "year_t1" = "year"))
```

#### Seed to recruit model
```{r}
df_re_mod <- df_re %>%
  filter(nr_seeds > 0)

mod_re <- lm(
  nr_recruits ~ nr_seeds,
  data = df_re_mod)

summary(mod_re)

recr_intercept <- unname(coef(mod_re)[["(Intercept)"]])
recr_per_seed <- unname(coef(mod_re)[["nr_seeds"]])

```

```{r}
df_re_newdata <- tibble(

    max(df_re_mod$nr_seeds), length.out = 200))

df_re_newdata <- bind_cols(

  as_tibble(predict(
    mod_re, newdata = df_re_newdata,
    interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)))

fig_re <- ggplot(

  geom_line(

    aes(x = nr_seeds, y = fit),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Seed to recruit transition",
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x = expression("Number of seeds"[t]),
    y = expression("Number of recruits"[t+1])) +
  theme_bw()

fig_re
```

## Building the IPM from scratch
The IPM now includes a continuous size distribution for active individuals and two discrete states for dormant individuals and seeds. Active individuals may remain active, enter dormancy, or contribute seeds. Dormant individuals may survive and remain dormant or reactivate into the continuous size distribution.

The discrete seed state accounts for the two-year delay between seed production and recruitment. Seeds produced in year (t) enter the seed state in (t+1) and contribute new recruits in (t+2), according to the estimated seed-to-recruit rate and recruit size distribution.
```{r}
extr_value <- function(x, field) {
  subset(x, coefficient == field)$value}

# Reference active abundance in the recruitment-fitting population-years.
df_re_n <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(persistence_t0), persistence_t0 != 'DEAD', dormant_t0 == 0) %>%
  group_by(population, year) %>%
  summarise(n_active = n_distinct(id), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  semi_join(df_re_mod, by = c('population', 'year'))

pars <- Filter(
  function(x) length(x) > 0,
  list(
    prefix = v_script_prefix,
    species = v_species,
    
    surv_b0 = extr_value(pars_su, 'b0'),
    surv_b1 = extr_value(pars_su, 'logsize_t0'),
    surv_b2 = extr_value(pars_su, 'logsize_t0_2'),
    surv_b3 = extr_value(pars_su, 'logsize_t0_3'),
    
    grow_b0 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'b0'),
    grow_b1 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'logsize_t0'),
    grow_b2 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'logsize_t0_2'),
    grow_b3 = extr_value(pars_gr, 'logsize_t0_3'),
    a = extr_value(pars_gr, 'a'),
    b = extr_value(pars_gr, 'b'),
    
    dorm_b0 = extr_value(pars_do, 'b0'),
    dorm_b1 = extr_value(pars_do, 'logsize_t0'),
    dorm_b2 = extr_value(pars_do, 'logsize_t0_2'),
    dorm_b3 = extr_value(pars_do, 'logsize_t0_3'),
    
    flower_b0 = extr_value(pars_fl, 'b0'),
    flower_b1 = extr_value(pars_fl, 'logsize_t0'),
    flower_b2 = extr_value(pars_fl, 'logsize_t0_2'),
    flower_b3 = extr_value(pars_fl, 'logsize_t0_3'),
    
    seed_b0 = extr_value(pars_se, 'b0'),
    seed_b1 = extr_value(pars_se, 'logsize_t0'),
    seed_b2 = extr_value(pars_se, 'logsize_t0_2'),
    seed_b3 = extr_value(pars_se, 'logsize_t0_3'),
    
    seed_n_b0 = extr_value(pars_se_n, 'b0'),
    seed_n_b1 = extr_value(pars_se_n, 'logsize_t0'),
    seed_n_b2 = extr_value(pars_se_n, 'logsize_t0_2'),
    seed_n_b3 = extr_value(pars_se_n, 'logsize_t0_3'),
    
    recr_sz = extr_value(pars_other, 'recr_sz'),
    recr_sd = extr_value(pars_other, 'recr_sd'),
    recr_b0 = unname(coef(mod_re)[['(Intercept)']]),
    recr_per_seed = unname(coef(mod_re)[['nr_seeds']]),
    recr_n_ref = mean(df_re_n$n_active),
    
    react_b0 = extr_value(pars_other, 'react_b0'),
    react_b1 = extr_value(pars_other, 'react_b1'),
    react_sd = extr_value(pars_other, 'react_sd'),
    
    p_dorm_survival = extr_value(pars_other, 'p_dorm_survival'),
    p_reactivate_1 = extr_value(pars_other, 'p_reactivate_1'),
    
    L = extr_value(pars_other, 'min_siz'),
    U = extr_value(pars_other, 'max_siz'),
    mat_siz = 200,
    
    mod_gr_index = v_mod_gr_index,
    mod_su_index = v_mod_su_index,
    mod_do_index = v_mod_do_index,
    mod_fl_index = v_mod_fl_index,
    mod_se_index = v_mod_se_index,
    mod_se_n_index = v_mod_se_n_index))
```


## IPM functions
```{r}
grow_sd <- function(x, pars) {
  sqrt(pars$a * exp(pars$b * x))}


# Growth from size x to size y.
gxy <- function(x, y, pars, num_pars = v_mod_gr_index) {
  mean_value <- pars$grow_b0
  
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('grow_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        mean_value <- mean_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}}}
  
  sd_value <- grow_sd(x, pars)
  dnorm(y, mean = mean_value, sd = sd_value)}


inv_logit <- function(x) {
  plogis(x)}


# Survival of an x-sized active individual.
sx <- function(x, pars, num_pars = v_mod_su_index) {
  survival_value <- pars$surv_b0
  
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('surv_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        survival_value <- survival_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}}}
  
  inv_logit(survival_value)}


# Dormancy entry conditional on survival.
dx <- function(x, pars, num_pars = v_mod_do_index) {
  dorm_value <- pars$dorm_b0
  
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('dorm_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        dorm_value <- dorm_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}}}
  
  inv_logit(dorm_value)}


# Flowering probability.
flx <- function(x, pars, num_pars = v_mod_fl_index) {
  flower_value <- pars$flower_b0
  
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('flower_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        flower_value <- flower_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}}}
  
  inv_logit(flower_value)}


# Positive seed production conditional on flowering.
sex <- function(x, pars, num_pars = v_mod_se_index) {
  seed_value <- pars$seed_b0
  
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('seed_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        seed_value <- seed_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}}}
  
  inv_logit(seed_value)}


# Seed number conditional on positive seed production.
se_nx <- function(x, pars, num_pars = v_mod_se_n_index) {
  seed_n_value <- pars$seed_n_b0
  
  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0('seed_n_b', i)
      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        seed_n_value <- seed_n_value + pars[[param_name]] * x^i}}}
  
  exp(seed_n_value)}


# Expected seed production of an active individual.
seedx <- function(x, pars) {
  flx(x, pars) * sex(x, pars) * se_nx(x, pars)}


# Active survival-growth transition.
pxy <- function(x, y, pars) {
  sx(x, pars) * (1 - dx(x, pars)) * gxy(x, y, pars)}
```

## Kernel
```{r}
# Rows = destinations; columns = sources.
# 1:n = active; (n+1):(2*n) = D1; (2*n+1):(3*n) = D2.
# Both dormant stages retain size before dormancy.
kernel <- function(pars) {
  n <- pars$mat_siz
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])
  
  i_dorm1 <- n + seq_len(n)
  i_dorm2 <- 2 * n + seq_len(n)
  
  # Growth distribution
  Gmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Gmat[] <- t(outer(y, y, gxy, pars)) * h
  
  # Eviction correction
  for (i in seq_len(n / 2)) {
    Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])}
  
  for (i in ((n / 2) + 1):n) {
    Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])}
  
  # Active survival and dormancy entry
  Smat <- sx(y, pars)
  Dvec <- dx(y, pars)
  Tmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i] * (1 - Dvec[i])}
  
  # Reactivation size conditional on entry size
  react_sd_use <- max(h / 10, pars$react_sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  Rmat <- vapply(y, function(x) {
    react_y <- dnorm(
      y, mean = pars$react_b0 + pars$react_b1 * x,
      sd = react_sd_use, log = TRUE)
    react_y <- exp(react_y - max(react_y))
    react_y / sum(react_y)}, numeric(n))
  
  # Recruit size distribution
  recr_sd_use <- max(h / 10, pars$recr_sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  recr_y <- dnorm(y, mean = pars$recr_sz, sd = recr_sd_use) * h
  recr_y <- recr_y / sum(recr_y)
  
  Pmat <- matrix(0, 3 * n, 3 * n)
  Fmat <- matrix(0, 3 * n, 3 * n)
  
  # Active -> active
  Pmat[1:n, 1:n] <- Tmat
  
  # Active -> D1: retain entry size.
  Pmat[i_dorm1, 1:n] <- diag(Smat * Dvec, nrow = n, ncol = n)
  
  # D1 -> active
  Pmat[1:n, i_dorm1] <-
    pars$p_dorm_survival * pars$p_reactivate_1 * Rmat
  
  # D1 -> D2: retain the same entry size.
  Pmat[i_dorm2, i_dorm1] <- diag(
    pars$p_dorm_survival * (1 - pars$p_reactivate_1), nrow = n, ncol = n)
  
  # D2 -> active: all surviving plants reactivate.
  Pmat[1:n, i_dorm2] <- pars$p_dorm_survival * Rmat
  
  # Population intercept allocated per active plant at reference abundance.
  Fmat[1:n, 1:n] <- outer(
    recr_y,
    pars$recr_b0 / pars$recr_n_ref + pars$recr_per_seed * seedx(y, pars))
  
  k_yx <- Pmat + Fmat
  
  list(
    k_yx = k_yx, Pmat = Pmat, Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat, Gmat = Gmat, Rmat = Rmat,
    meshpts = y,
    dormant_index = c(i_dorm1, i_dorm2),
    dormant1_index = i_dorm1,
    dormant2_index = i_dorm2)}


lambda_ipm <- function(i) {
  Re(eigen(kernel(i)$k_yx)$values[1])}
```

## Mean IPM population growth rate
```{r}
lam_mean <- lambda_ipm(pars)
lam_mean
```

## Building the IPM with ipmr
```{r}
proto_ipm_p <- init_ipm(
  sim_gen = 'general', di_dd = 'di', det_stoch = 'det') %>%
  
  # Active -> active
  define_kernel(
    name = 'P',
    family = 'CC',
    formula = s * (1 - p_do) * g * d_size,
    
    s = plogis(
      surv_b0 +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 1) surv_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 2) surv_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 3) surv_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    p_do = plogis(
      dorm_b0 +
        (if (mod_do_index >= 1) dorm_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_do_index >= 2) dorm_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_do_index >= 3) dorm_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    mu_g = grow_b0 +
      (if (mod_gr_index >= 1) grow_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
      (if (mod_gr_index >= 2) grow_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
      (if (mod_gr_index >= 3) grow_b3 * size_1^3 else 0),
    
    g = dnorm(size_2, mu_g, grow_sig),
    grow_sig = sqrt(a * exp(b * size_1)),
    
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('size')),
    uses_par_sets = FALSE,
    evict_cor = TRUE,
    evict_fun = truncated_distributions(fun = 'norm', target = 'g')) %>%
  
  # Active -> D1
  define_kernel(
    name = 'D_enter',
    family = 'CC',
    formula = s * p_do * entry_memory * d_size,
    
    entry_memory = as.numeric(size_1 == dorm1_2) / d_size,
    
    s = plogis(
      surv_b0 +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 1) surv_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 2) surv_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_su_index >= 3) surv_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    p_do = plogis(
      dorm_b0 +
        (if (mod_do_index >= 1) dorm_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_do_index >= 2) dorm_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_do_index >= 3) dorm_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('size', 'dorm1')),
    uses_par_sets = FALSE,
    evict_cor = FALSE) %>%
  
  # D1 -> D2
  define_kernel(
    name = 'D_advance',
    family = 'CC',
    formula =
      p_dorm_survival * (1 - p_reactivate_1) * entry_memory * d_dorm1,
    
    entry_memory = as.numeric(dorm1_1 == dorm2_2) / d_dorm1,
    
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('dorm1', 'dorm2')),
    uses_par_sets = FALSE,
    evict_cor = FALSE) %>%
  
  # D1 -> active
  define_kernel(
    name = 'D_leave1',
    family = 'CC',
    formula = p_dorm_survival * p_reactivate_1 * r_d * d_dorm1,
    
    react_mu = react_b0 + react_b1 * dorm1_1,
    react_sig = max(d_size / 10, react_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_d = dnorm(size_2, react_mu, react_sig),
    
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('dorm1', 'size')),
    uses_par_sets = FALSE,
    evict_cor = TRUE,
    evict_fun = truncated_distributions(fun = 'norm', target = 'r_d')) %>%
  
  # D2 -> active
  define_kernel(
    name = 'D_leave2',
    family = 'CC',
    formula = p_dorm_survival * r_d * d_dorm2,
    
    react_mu = react_b0 + react_b1 * dorm2_1,
    react_sig = max(d_size / 10, react_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_d = dnorm(size_2, react_mu, react_sig),
    
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('dorm2', 'size')),
    uses_par_sets = FALSE,
    evict_cor = TRUE,
    evict_fun = truncated_distributions(fun = 'norm', target = 'r_d')) %>%
  
  # Active -> recruits: intercept and seed production both contribute.
  define_kernel(
    name = 'F',
    family = 'CC',
    formula =
      (recr_b0 / recr_n_ref + p_fl * p_se * n_se * recr_per_seed) *
      r_d * d_size,
    
    p_fl = plogis(
      flower_b0 +
        (if (mod_fl_index >= 1) flower_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_fl_index >= 2) flower_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_fl_index >= 3) flower_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    p_se = plogis(
      seed_b0 +
        (if (mod_se_index >= 1) seed_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_se_index >= 2) seed_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_se_index >= 3) seed_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    n_se = exp(
      seed_n_b0 +
        (if (mod_se_n_index >= 1) seed_n_b1 * size_1 else 0) +
        (if (mod_se_n_index >= 2) seed_n_b2 * size_1^2 else 0) +
        (if (mod_se_n_index >= 3) seed_n_b3 * size_1^3 else 0)),
    
    recr_sig = max(d_size / 10, recr_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_d = dnorm(size_2, recr_sz, recr_sig),
    
    data_list = pars,
    states = list(c('size')),
    uses_par_sets = FALSE,
    evict_cor = TRUE,
    evict_fun = truncated_distributions(fun = 'norm', target = 'r_d')) %>%
  
  # Kernel implementation
  define_impl(
    make_impl_args_list(
      kernel_names = c(
        'P', 'D_enter', 'D_advance', 'D_leave1', 'D_leave2', 'F'),
      int_rule = rep('midpoint', 6),
      state_start = c('size', 'size', 'dorm1', 'dorm1', 'dorm2', 'size'),
      state_end = c('size', 'dorm1', 'dorm2', 'size', 'size', 'size'))) %>%
  
  # Domains
  define_domains(
    size = c(pars$L, pars$U, pars$mat_siz),
    dorm1 = c(pars$L, pars$U, pars$mat_siz),
    dorm2 = c(pars$L, pars$U, pars$mat_siz)) %>%
  
  # Initial population
  define_pop_state(
    pop_vectors = list(
      n_size = rep(1 / pars$mat_siz, pars$mat_siz),
      n_dorm1 = rep(0, pars$mat_siz),
      n_dorm2 = rep(0, pars$mat_siz)))


ipmr_p <- make_ipm(proto_ipm = proto_ipm_p, iterations = 200)


# Mean IPM population growth rate ---------------------------------------------
lam_mean_ipmr <- lambda(ipmr_p)
lam_mean_ipmr


# Compare hand-built and ipmr implementations ----------------------------------
lam_mean_ipmr

```

# Yearly IPM, basic {#ipm_yr_zero}

## Introduction
In this chapter, we extend the basic mean IPM to account for year-to-year variation in survival, growth, and recruitment. We use mixed-effects models to estimate year-specific vital rates while retaining the same continuous size structure and size-independent recruitment. We then construct year-specific IPMs and compare their asymptotic growth rates and one-step population projections with observed population growth.

## Specifications
```{r}
v_mod_set_su <- c()
v_mod_set_gr <- c()

# Controls
ctrl_glmer <- glmerControl(
  optimizer = 'bobyqa',
  optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))

ctrl_lmer <- lmerControl(
  optimizer = 'bobyqa',
  optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
```

## Data
```{r}
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0(v_head, '_', v_sp_abb, '_df_workdata.csv'))) %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year)) %>%
  filter(
    state == v_states,
    !is.na(year),
    !(year %in% v_years_re))
```

## Vital rates
For survival and growth, we consider the same four model structures as in the basic mean IPM: intercept-only, linear, quadratic, and cubic relationships with log leaf area. Model selection is based on AICc, with the option to manually specify a model instead.

To account for temporal variation, we include year as a random intercept in the survival model and allow both the intercept and the linear size effect to vary among years in the growth model.

### Survival
#### Data
```{r}
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    reliable_demography,
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0)) %>%
  mutate(
    year = factor(year)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, id, year, size_t0, survives,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)
```

#### Model
```{r}
mod_su_0 <- glmer(
  survives ~ 1 + (1 | year),
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial,
  control = ctrl_glmer)

mod_su_1 <- glmer(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + (1 | year),
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial,
  control = ctrl_glmer)

mod_su_2 <- glmer(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + (1 | year),
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial,
  control = ctrl_glmer)

mod_su_3 <- glmer(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3 +
    (1 | year),
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial,
  control = ctrl_glmer)

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_0, mod_su_1, mod_su_2, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_su,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- mods_su_sorted[1]
  v_mod_su_index <- mod_su_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_su + 1
  v_mod_su_index <- v_mod_set_su}

mod_su_best <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_bestfit]]
mod_su_ranef <- coef(mod_su_best)$year

mod_su_best
summary(mod_su_best)
mods_su_dAICc
```

#### Plots by year
```{r}
make_su_year_plot <- function(year_i) {
  df_i <- df_su %>%
    filter(year == year_i)

  x <- seq(
    min(df_i$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    max(df_i$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    length.out = 100)

  pred_i <- tibble(
    logsize_t0 = x) %>%
    mutate(
      logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
      logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3,
      year = factor(
        year_i,
        levels = levels(df_su$year)))

  pred_i$survives <- predict(
    mod_su_best,
    newdata = pred_i,
    type = 'response',
    re.form = NULL)

  pts_i <- df_i %>%
    mutate(
      bin = cut(
        logsize_t0,
        breaks = 8)) %>%
    group_by(bin) %>%
    summarise(
      logsize_t0 = mean(logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
      survives = mean(survives, na.rm = TRUE),
      n = n(),
      .groups = 'drop') %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(logsize_t0),
      n > 0)

  ggplot() +
    geom_point(
      data = pts_i,
      aes(logsize_t0, survives),
      size = 1.1) +
    geom_line(
      data = pred_i,
      aes(logsize_t0, survives),
      linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(
      title = year_i,
      x = expression('log(leaf area)'[t0]),
      y = expression('Survival probability'[t1])) +
    ylim(0, 1) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      text = element_text(size = 5),
      legend.position = 'none')
}

su_yrs <- lapply(
  levels(df_su$year),
  make_su_year_plot)

fig_su_years <- wrap_plots(su_yrs) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = 'Survival - year specific',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        size = 13,
        face = 'bold'),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(
        size = 9)))

fig_su_years
```

### Growth
#### Data
```{r}
df_gr <- df %>%
  filter(
    consecutive,
    size_t0 > 0,
    size_t1 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0),
    is.finite(logsize_t1)) %>%
  mutate(
    year = factor(year)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, id, year, size_t0, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)
```

#### Model
```{r}
mod_gr_0 <- lmer(
  logsize_t1 ~ 1 + (logsize_t0 | year),
  data = df_gr,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = ctrl_lmer)

mod_gr_1 <- lmer(
  logsize_t1 ~ logsize_t0 + (logsize_t0 | year),
  data = df_gr,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = ctrl_lmer)

mod_gr_2 <- lmer(
  logsize_t1 ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 +
    (logsize_t0 | year),
  data = df_gr,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = ctrl_lmer)

mod_gr_3 <- lmer(
  logsize_t1 ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3 +
    (logsize_t0 | year),
  data = df_gr,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = ctrl_lmer)

mods_gr <- list(
  mod_gr_0, mod_gr_1, mod_gr_2, mod_gr_3)

mods_gr_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_gr,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_gr_sorted <- order(mods_gr_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_gr) == 0) {
  mod_gr_index_bestfit <- mods_gr_sorted[1]
  v_mod_gr_index <- mod_gr_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_gr_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_gr + 1
  v_mod_gr_index <- v_mod_set_gr}

mod_gr_best <- mods_gr[[mod_gr_index_bestfit]]
mod_gr_ranef <- coef(mod_gr_best)$year

mod_gr_best
summary(mod_gr_best)
mods_gr_dAICc
```

#### Plots
```{r}
make_gr_year_plot <- function(year_i) {
  df_i <- df_gr %>%
    filter(year == year_i)

  x <- seq(
    min(df_i$logsize_t0, na.rm = TRUE),

  pred_i$logsize_t1 <- predict(

  ggplot() +
```

### Growth variance
```{r}
mod_gr_x <- fitted(mod_gr_best)
mod_gr_y <- resid(mod_gr_best)^2

mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x),
  start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(
    maxiter = 1000,
    tol = 1e-6,
    warnOnly = TRUE))
```

### Recruitment
Recruitment is estimated at the population-year level, following the same approach as in the basic mean IPM. However, we now include a random intercept for recruitment year (t+1), allowing the expected number of recruits per established individual to vary among years.

The resulting year-specific recruitment rates are applied uniformly across all parent sizes.
```{r}
# Constant recruitment per established plant with a recruit-year random effect.

df_re_parent <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(persistence_t0),
    persistence_t0 != 'DEAD',
    size_t0 > 0) %>%
  group_by(
    population,
    year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_parents = n_distinct(id),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = year + 1L)

df_re_sampled <- df %>%
  distinct(
    population,
    year) %>%
  rename(
    year_t1 = year)

df_re_count <- df %>%
  filter(
    recruit == 1) %>%
  count(
    population,
    year,
    name = 'nr_recruits') %>%
  rename(
    year_t1 = year)

df_re <- df_re_parent %>%
  inner_join(
    df_re_sampled,
    by = c(
      'population',
      'year_t1')) %>%
  left_join(
    df_re_count,
    by = c(
      'population',
      'year_t1')) %>%
  mutate(
    nr_recruits = replace_na(
      nr_recruits,
      0L),
    year_t1 = factor(year_t1))

mod_re <- glmer.nb(
  nr_recruits ~ 1 + offset(log(n_parents)) +
    (1 | year_t1),
  data = df_re,
  control = ctrl_glmer)

mod_re_ranef <- coef(mod_re)$year_t1

mod_re
summary(mod_re)

fecu_mean <- exp(
  unname(
    fixef(mod_re)[['(Intercept)']]))
```

## Parameter extraction
We extract both fixed-effect and year-specific parameter estimates from the fitted models. Survival and growth parameters are associated with the initial year (t), while recruitment parameters correspond to the following year (t+1), when seedlings are observed.

Growth variance and the recruit size distribution remain constant across years.
```{r}
get_coef <- function(x, name) {
  if (name %in% names(x)) {
    unname(x[[name]])
  } else {
    0
  }
}


# Mean parameters -------------------------------------------------------------
su_fix <- fixef(mod_su_best)
gr_fix <- fixef(mod_gr_best)
gr_var_coef <- coef(mod_gr_var)

pars_mean <- list(
  prefix = v_script_prefix,
  species = v_species,

  surv_b0 = get_coef(
    su_fix,
    '(Intercept)'),
  surv_b1 = get_coef(
    su_fix,
    'logsize_t0'),
  surv_b2 = get_coef(
    su_fix,
    'logsize_t0_2'),
  surv_b3 = get_coef(
    su_fix,
    'logsize_t0_3'),

  grow_b0 = get_coef(
    gr_fix,
    '(Intercept)'),
  grow_b1 = get_coef(
    gr_fix,
    'logsize_t0'),
  grow_b2 = get_coef(
    gr_fix,
    'logsize_t0_2'),
  grow_b3 = get_coef(
    gr_fix,
    'logsize_t0_3'),

  a = as.numeric(
    gr_var_coef[1]),
  b = as.numeric(
    gr_var_coef[2]),

  fecu_b0 = fecu_mean,

  recr_sz = mean(
    df_re_size$logsize_t0,
    na.rm = TRUE),
  recr_sd = sd(
    df_re_size$logsize_t0,
    na.rm = TRUE),

  L = min(
    df_gr$logsize_t0,
    na.rm = TRUE),
  U = max(
    df_gr$logsize_t0,
    na.rm = TRUE),
  mat_siz = 200,

  mod_gr_index = v_mod_gr_index,
  mod_su_index = v_mod_su_index)


# Year-specific parameters ----------------------------------------------------
make_ipm_pars <- function(
    year,
    re_year_t1 = NULL) {

  pars <- pars_mean
  year <- as.character(year)

  if (year %in% rownames(mod_su_ranef)) {
    pars$surv_b0 <- get_coef(
      mod_su_ranef[year, ],
      '(Intercept)')
    pars$surv_b1 <- get_coef(
      mod_su_ranef[year, ],
      'logsize_t0')
    pars$surv_b2 <- get_coef(
      mod_su_ranef[year, ],
      'logsize_t0_2')
    pars$surv_b3 <- get_coef(
      mod_su_ranef[year, ],
      'logsize_t0_3')
  }

  if (year %in% rownames(mod_gr_ranef)) {
    pars$grow_b0 <- get_coef(
      mod_gr_ranef[year, ],
      '(Intercept)')
    pars$grow_b1 <- get_coef(
      mod_gr_ranef[year, ],
      'logsize_t0')
    pars$grow_b2 <- get_coef(
      mod_gr_ranef[year, ],
      'logsize_t0_2')
    pars$grow_b3 <- get_coef(
      mod_gr_ranef[year, ],
      'logsize_t0_3')
  }

  if (is.null(re_year_t1)) {
    re_year_t1 <- as.integer(year) + 1L
  }

  re_year_t1 <- as.character(re_year_t1)

  if (re_year_t1 %in% rownames(mod_re_ranef)) {
    pars$fecu_b0 <- exp(
      get_coef(
        mod_re_ranef[re_year_t1, ],
        '(Intercept)'))
  }

  pars
}
```

## IPM functions
```{r}
grow_sd <- function(x, pars) {
  sqrt(
    pars$a *
      exp(pars$b * x))
}


# Growth from size x to size y.
gxy <- function(
    x,
    y,
    pars,
    num_pars = v_mod_gr_index) {

  mean_value <- 0

  for (i in 0:num_pars) {
    param_name <- paste0(
      'grow_b',
      i)

    if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
      mean_value <- mean_value +
        pars[[param_name]] *
        x^i
    }
  }

  sd_value <- grow_sd(
    x,
    pars)

  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = mean_value,
    sd = sd_value)
}


inv_logit <- function(x) {
  exp(x) /
    (1 + exp(x))
}


# Survival of an x-sized individual to t1.
sx <- function(
    x,
    pars,
    num_pars = v_mod_su_index) {

  survival_value <- pars$surv_b0

  if (num_pars >= 1) {
    for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
      param_name <- paste0(
        'surv_b',
        i)

      if (!is.null(pars[[param_name]])) {
        survival_value <- survival_value +
          pars[[param_name]] *
          x^i
      }
    }
  }

  inv_logit(
    survival_value)
}


# Survival-growth transition.
pxy <- function(
    x,
    y,
    pars) {

  sx(
    x,
    pars) *
    gxy(
      x,
      y,
      pars)
}


# Constant fecundity distributed across recruit sizes.
fy <- function(
    y,
    pars,
    h) {

  n_recr <- pars$fecu_b0

  recr_sd <- max(
    h / 10,
    pars$recr_sd,
    na.rm = TRUE)

  recr_y <- dnorm(
    y,
    pars$recr_sz,
    recr_sd) * h

  recr_y <- recr_y /
    sum(recr_y)

  n_recr *
    recr_y
}
```

## Kernel
We retain the same kernel structure as in the basic mean IPM, using 200 mesh points and separate survival-growth and recruitment components. For each year, we update the vital-rate parameters using the corresponding year-specific estimates.
```{r}
kernel <- function(pars) {
  n <- pars$mat_siz
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 *
    (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  Fmat <- matrix(
    0,
    n,
    n)

  Fmat[] <- matrix(
    fy(
      y,
      pars,
      h),
    n,
    n)

  Smat <- sx(
    y,
    pars)

  Gmat <- matrix(
    0,
    n,
    n)

  Gmat[] <- t(
    outer(
      y,
      y,
      gxy,
      pars)) * h

  Tmat <- matrix(
    0,
    n,
    n)

  for (i in seq_len(n / 2)) {
    Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] +
      1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] *
      Smat[i]
  }

  for (i in ((n / 2) + 1):n) {
    Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] +
      1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] *
      Smat[i]
  }

  k_yx <- Fmat +
    Tmat

  list(
    k_yx = k_yx,
    Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat,
    Gmat = Gmat,
    meshpts = y,
    h = h,
    L = L,
    U = U)
}


lambda_ipm <- function(pars) {
  Re(
    eigen(
      kernel(pars)$k_yx)$values[1])
}
```
